Mr. Chairman, over the past decade, humanity's access and operations in outer space have fundamentally changed, and the driving factors behind these changes are likely to accelerate in the coming decades. This change presents us opportunities and risks, and we need to develop further the existing governance so that we can sustainably accelerate innovation and discovery with a view to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. It is our shared responsibility to ensure that existing international space law is fully implemented and that effective governance is in place to propel innovation and mitigate risks. Greece strongly believes that the 5 UN treaties on outer space and the relevant UN General Assembly sets of principles constitute the cornerstone of international space law. In this context, Greece considers COPUOS and its subcommittees as the main fora for the development of international space law guidelines, best practices, confidence-building measures, policy issues, and international cooperation. As to international cooperation in particular, we believe that it should by all means prevail over any use of force in space. We welcome in this regard the adoption by the UN General Assembly of Resolution 79/87 of 2024 on international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space, which among other things expresses its serious concern about the possibility of an armed race in outer space, stresses the importance of Article 4 of the Outer Space Treaty, and reaffirms the significance of international cooperation in developing the relevant norms of international space law for a space free from arms race and conflict. The importance of international cooperation was also solemnly confirmed in Action 56 of Resolution 79/1 of 2024 on the Pact for the Future. Mr. Chairman, the Corpus Legal Subcommittee has proven its ability to deliver on its mandate and should continue to be the primary forum for the discussions on an international legal framework for the development of space resource activities. In developing such a legal framework, the Working Group on Space Resources could be guided and use as a tool the long-established solid international legal practice adopted within the framework of specialized agencies of the UN system, part of which is also COPUOS, such as the administration of international seabed by the International Seabed Authority in accordance with the UNCLOS, or the frequency spectrum management regime of the ITU and the legal regime governing Antarctica. Mr. Chairman, allow me to give you, in addition, a brief insight into my country's endeavors in the space sector. The Greek space law establishes the legal framework for the authorization of space activities and provides among other things, for the procedure for the licensing of space activities and their registration to the National Space Registry. The Greek Space Law has been revised in 2024 in order to provide for a third-party liability amount requested by the satellite operators as a mandatory condition. Through this legislative approach, the growth of the small satellite sector is encouraged. Greece has recently enacted a specific national regulatory framework describing the procedures to be followed by companies and other organizations for the management and processing of satellite filings that are submitted through Greece to the ITU. Furthermore, my country is steadily proceeding with the implementation, in collaboration with ESA, of its national microsatellite program that includes the construction and launch of 13 satellites of various types covering identified national needs, such as natural disaster monitoring, security, and environmental protection. The upcoming fleet of Greek satellites consists of 7 microsatellites with optical payload and capabilities of very high-resolution imaging, 4 dedicated thermal microsatellites with sensors that monitor thermal emissions and can detect fire fronts under thick smoke or during the night, and 2 high-resolution synthetic aperture radar microsatellites that can observe the ground and sea surface under thick clouds and dark. Apart from the purely operational space and ground assets, Greece is investing in a set of experimental satellites, CubeSats, with the main objective to gain experience from in-orbit validation through a proof-of-concept process, enhancing the collective capabilities of Greek space ecosystem and laying the groundwork for the future development of few fully operational space missions. Mr. Chairman, in concluding, let me assure you that Greece will continue to intensively work for the promotion and deepening of international cooperation in the space domain and the conduct of space activities in accordance with international law as required by Article 3 of the Outer Space Treaty. I thank you.

At this moment, we would also like to extend our sincere condolences to the delegation of Poland for the loss of Ambassador Andrzej Miszczak, a visionary diplomat We note with appreciation that the initial draft set of recommended principles for space resource activities recognizes the existence of human cultural heritage in space. We are grateful and firmly support the submissions of Poland and the United Kingdom to the ATLAS, which also encouraged the action team to prioritize cultural heritage during its consultations. We believe that the 1960s The 1967 Outer Space Treaty provides a legal foundation for heritage protection. While Article 1 assures free access to all areas of celestial bodies and Article 2 bans national appropriation, Article 9 requires application of due regard when engaged in space activities. Broad multilateral consultations are required to avoid harmful interference. Similarly, Article 12 suggests that access may be guided by considerations of reciprocity. Taken together, these principles can provide for managed protocols that balance access with the necessity to safeguard. Managed access protocols must be science-based and should be established through consensus by the COPUSS member states. To assist this effort, the innovative For All Mankind's Moon Registry A digital catalog of the more than 115 sites on the Moon which bear evidence of human activity offers an inventory of sites that may be identified and prioritized for safeguarding by COPOS member states. Our space law and heritage law experts from various countries, including Poland, Nigeria, Italy, Qatar, Greece, and Mexico are eager to offer their expertise to assist the COPOS member states in their consideration of the potential identification and safeguarding measures of cultural sites on the Moon. On Earth, the 1972 UNESCO World Heritage Convention provides a process by which to protect sites of outstanding universal value as essential to human identity and sustainable development by identifying, safeguarding, and preserving irreplaceable cultural heritage that As citizens beyond Earth, we revere the accomplishments of past generations. Sites of Outstanding Universal Value include humanity's first lunar landing sites, which represent shared human achievements that should be safeguarded in recognition and celebration of human ingenuity and the collaborative spirit of space exploration. Just like their counterparts on Earth, they represent masterpieces of human creative genius, are an outstanding example of a technological ensemble or landscape which reflects significant stages in human history, and are directly or tangibly associated with events and ideas of outstanding universal significance. However, unlike terrestrial heritage, sites in outer space lack a protective framework. The 1972 UNESCO World Heritage Convention relies on state sovereignty as part of its nomination process, but Article 2 of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits national appropriation of territory in outer space, making this model inapplicable. Indeed, no international mechanism currently defines, safeguards, or manages any sites in outer space, leaving all of them, whether of scientific, cultural, or commercial value, vulnerable to damage and interference as missions multiply. This gasp— this gap, sorry, risks escalating tensions over access and use of space resources and the sites where those resources can be found, necessitating a new approach to ensure sustainability and cooperation. Under the UN regime, a legal and diplomatic scheme to identify and safeguard cultural heritage sites beyond Earth, and thus beyond national jurisdiction, must be led and developed by the member states of the UN COPUIS. The concept of managed access protocols can be found in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. Article 1 designates the exploration and use of outer space as the province of all humankind and enshrines the right to freely access all areas of celestial bodies. Article 2 of the treaty bans national appropriation of space, including the moon and other celestial bodies. Together, these principles ensure equitable access and peaceful cooperation, but pose challenges for implementing protective measures to manage competing interests. For example, restricting access to specific areas of scientific or cultural significance could be seen as limiting the freedom of exploration and use guaranteed by Article 1, or as a form of appropriation under Article 2. However, protective measures can be designed as non-sovereign stewardship measures, such as temporary access restrictions, to mitigate conflict without violating treaty obligations. Such measures would foster cooperation by ensuring that scientific and commercial activities respect shared interests. Article 9 of the Outer Space Treaty offers a legal basis for conflict prevention by requiring states to conduct activities with due regard for others' interests and to avoid harmful contamination of celestial bodies. It also requires consultation in the anticipation of harmful interference. Similarly, Article 12, which mandates reciprocal access to installations on celestial bodies, highlights the importance of managed access protocols to balance transparency with the need to safeguard fragile sites, reducing the risk of conflict over access rights. Taken together, these provisions, which promote cooperation and transparency, suggest that the treaty supports the use of managed access protocols to balance free access with collectively decided safeguarding measures. Developing a framework within the UN COPUIS to identify and safeguard heritage sites can help establish collaborative procedures utilizing diplomatic, scientific, and legal means to facilitate the advancements of complex space laws. The real results would be to safeguard humanity's milestones, promote peaceful collaboration for access and use, support sustainability by fostering long-term cooperation, and serve as a model for broader safety and access protocols applicable to scientific, commercial, or resource extraction sites, building confidence in managing competing interests. These temporary protections are not permanent restrictions but flexible, time-bound measures that would allow the international community to develop lasting guidelines for space resource activities while protecting vulnerable sites during this critical period of increased activity. But this must be done in a manner that ensures people and property and the environment are not harmed. Next slide. These legal interests are addressed in paragraph 2 of guideline 6 of the Space degree mitigation guidelines. Additionally, the long-term sustainability guidelines address the risk to people, property, and the environment associated with space activities, including reentry in guideline A2. As long as a reentry is carefully controlled such that most of the spacecraft burns up in the atmosphere and heat-resistant components are directed to the so-called South Pacific Oceanic uninhabited area around Point Nemo, it poses no risk to people, property, or the environment.

However, the guidelines are part of non-binding international law. The legal challenges related to protecting people and property are primarily addressed in the Liability Convention, which provides a legally binding international framework for assigning responsibility in cases of damage caused by space objects. After all, even in a controlled reentry, surviving fragments may scatter unpredictably over a wide area, posing a small but real risk. Historical cases illustrate this uncertainty. For example, debris from Skylab, as shown on one of the previous slides, scattered across the southern coast of Western Australia after NASA missed its intended target in the Indian Ocean. While the risk of injury or damage from falling space debris is very low, it's not negligible. Next slide. Article 9 of the Outer Space Treaty obligates state parties not only to avoid harmful contamination of outer space, but also to avoid adverse changes in the environment of the Earth. However, a key issue arises with this provision. It only applies to impacts caused by the introduction of extraterrestrial matter. Since space debris is manmade, it does not fall under this category. This means that state parties, when engaging in exploration and the use of outer space, are not required by Article 9 to prevent harmful effects from space debris on Earth environment. Similarly, they have no obligation to adopt appropriate measures to avoid environmental impacts. Nevertheless, the provision reflects a clear underlying principle within the treaty: the responsibility to protect Earth environment from the negative effects of space activities, including the orbiting missions. Next slide. At the 40th session of this subcommittee in 2001, Latin American countries comprising the Rio Group raised concerns about the environmental risk of the orbiting and called for a legal regime to address environmental issues. Almost 25 years later, space law still contains no binding obligation to conduct environmental impact assessments. But what if we examine this issue through the lens of the law of the sea? From the law of the sea perspective, the relevant framework is the Convention on the Law of the Sea, particularly Part 12. Article 192 establishes a general duty to protect and preserve the marine environment, while Article 194 requires measures to control pollution from any source. Article 210 specifically explicitly regulates pollution by dumping. The question is whether deorbiting space objects into the ocean constitutes pollution under Article 1. Regardless of that, environmental assessments under the convention are only triggered when there is a risk of significant harm. Whether or not deorbiting large space objects meets that threshold, it is important to interpret Part 12 in the light of Article 194, which makes explicit reference to rare and fragile ecosystems as well as the habitat of depleted, threatened, and endangered species. Point Nemo is not necessarily such an area. More recently, the environmental implications have been considered in the BBNJ Agreement, also known as the High Seas Treaty. This new treaty aims to protect marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction. As of now, 114 states have signed and 21 have ratified. 60 ratifications are required for it to enter into force. The treaty remains open for signature until September 20, 2025. Article 29 of the treaty promotes the use of environmental impact assessments, while Article 30 sets thresholds for when a screening and an environmental impact assessment are required. These thresholds range from substantial to even minor or transitory environmental effects, which could apply to deorbiting. However, it remains unclear whether such activities meet these thresholds, and of course, whether the agreement will enter into force. In summary, there is currently no legally binding international framework that directly addresses the environmental impact of deorbiting space objects. However, the 1972 London Convention and its 1996 Protocol, which regulate and restrict ocean dumping, could be potential venues for addressing this issue in maritime law. Next slide. To put things into perspective, orbital reentries are not yet a major source of ocean pollution. For comparison, the total mass reentered from orbit is still less than that of a sunken World War II battleship, and over 2,000 garbage trucks of plastic enter the ocean every single day. Since 1971, just over 260 space objects have been deorbited to Point Nemo. While this impact remains small, it is not just about the ISS or one day the Tangzhong space station.
